suggestions.rationale: Active acromegaly with chronic GH/IGF-I excess is associated with hypertension through several disease-specific mechanisms, including direct renal sodium and water retention with extracellular-volume expansion and vascular effects. The 2026 acromegaly complications consensus reports that GH acts on distal-nephron epithelial sodium channels, that GH promotes nephron sodium retention and expanded extracellular water, and that biochemical control can lower blood pressure in hypertensive patients. This supports a direct-secondary research pathway when acromegaly activity and blood-pressure chronology are documented; it does not establish that every case of hypertension in a person with acromegaly is attributable to acromegaly.

pathwayIntelligence.causalChain: Biochemically active acromegaly with sustained GH/IGF-I excess → renal sodium/water retention and extracellular-volume expansion, with additional vascular/metabolic contributors → hypertension.
developmentQuestions: Was acromegaly objectively established with age-adjusted IGF-I, GH testing, and pituitary evaluation, and when was active disease documented?
When did sustained hypertension begin relative to active acromegaly?
Did blood pressure change after surgery or biochemical control of GH/IGF-I excess?
Are obstructive sleep apnea, insulin resistance, obesity, kidney disease, medication effects, or another secondary cause contributing to hypertension?
What home, ambulatory, or longitudinal clinic blood-pressure data document the diagnosis and course?
issuesToResolve: Hypertension in acromegaly is multifactorial and may persist after biochemical remission, so an individual relationship still requires chronology and competing-cause review.
The pathway should not be inferred from the acromegaly label alone when biochemical disease activity is not documented.

evidenceGaps: Diagnostic and biochemical records confirming acromegaly and periods of active GH/IGF-I excess
Longitudinal blood-pressure records establishing hypertension onset and course
Acromegaly treatment and biochemical-response records, including blood-pressure response when documented
Evaluation of other primary or secondary contributors to hypertension
Clinician assessment of the individual endocrine-to-blood-pressure chronology

sourceReferences.citation: Giustina et al., Consensus on acromegaly complications: an update, Pituitary. 2026;29(3):76. doi:10.1007/s11102-026-01639-z. PMID 42050227
sourceReferences.note: International consensus update describes direct GH effects on distal-nephron sodium handling, extracellular-water expansion, hypertension as a major acromegaly comorbidity, and blood-pressure improvement with biochemical disease control; supports a disease-specific pathway while preserving individual competing-cause review.
